article_title: US imposes 25% tariffs on wide range of Chinese goods; Beijing vows retaliation
article_summary: Washington hits Chinese imports with fresh 25 percent duties; China warns of countermeasures.
article_text:
WASHINGTON/BEIJING, March 24 (Reuters) - The United States on Monday imposed 25 percent tariffs on a wide range of Chinese manufactured goods, drawing an immediate vow from Beijing to retaliate and sending global equity markets sharply lower.

President Donald Trump signed the executive order at the White House, describing the measures as essential to correcting what he called decades of unfair trade practices by China. The tariffs cover consumer electronics, machinery components, steel and aluminium products, and a range of industrial goods.

China's commerce ministry said Beijing "firmly opposes" the tariff measures and will take "all necessary countermeasures" to defend its legitimate rights and interests. State television said the government would respond in a "targeted, proportional" manner.

Global markets reacted sharply. European and Asian stocks fell between 1 and 2 percent, while U.S. futures also dropped. The dollar weakened against the euro and the yen as traders moved into safe-haven assets.

Multinational companies with deep supply chain ties to China warned of disruption. Tech giant Apple Inc said it was reviewing the potential impact on its global operations and was considering shifting some production to other countries. Apple shares fell 3.4 percent.

The tariffs represent the most significant escalation in U.S.-China trade tensions since Trump's first term, when tariffs on hundreds of billions of dollars of Chinese goods were imposed and later partially wound back under a Phase One trade deal in 2020.

Administration officials said the measures were prompted by what they described as China's failure to comply with the 2020 deal, its continued subsidies to state-owned enterprises, and alleged intellectual property theft.

The World Trade Organization's dispute settlement mechanism is widely seen as too slow and cumbersome to provide quick relief, but Beijing could file a formal complaint. A previous WTO ruling found U.S. tariffs from Trump's first term violated international trade rules, a ruling the U.S. did not comply with.

Economists were divided on the likely long-run impact. Some said the tariffs would encourage reshoring of manufacturing and reduce dependence on China. Others said the cost would be borne by American consumers in the form of higher prices.

"The short-term pain is real and immediate — prices go up, supply chains get disrupted," said Eswar Prasad, a Cornell University professor and former head of the IMF's China division. "Whether there is long-run gain depends on how forcefully the policy is applied and how other countries respond."

The European Union said it was monitoring the situation closely and would defend its own companies' interests if they were caught in any crossfire. Canada said it was in contact with Washington about the implications for North American supply chains.

In Beijing, state media called the tariffs a form of economic coercion and urged other countries to support rules-based global trade. Chinese social media users expressed anger, with calls for boycotts of American consumer products trending on Weibo.

The White House said further tariff increases remained possible if China did not engage in good-faith trade negotiations.
